en: Netti:
The Section on Detailed Exposition (Paṭiniddesavāra), Analysis 14.
The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Terms of Expression (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra-vibhaṅga). Therein, what is the mode of conveying terms of expression?
“Phenomena by way of unity, and those also demonstrated by way of diversity.”
Those which are specified therein should be understood accordingly.
"Suffering" is a state of oneness.
In that regard, what is suffering?
Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering;
association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the pleasant is suffering, not to obtain what one desires is suffering; in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Form is suffering, feeling is suffering, perception is suffering, mental formations are suffering, consciousness is suffering.
This is diversity.
"The origin of suffering" is unity.
In this regard, what is the origin of suffering?
It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there;
namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
This is diversity.
"The cessation of suffering" is unity.
In that regard, what is the cessation of suffering?
The remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving—its relinquishing, its renunciation, its liberation, its non-attachment:
this is diversity.
“The practice leading to the cessation of suffering”: this is unity.
In that regard, what is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path.
That is to say:
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—
this is diversity. "The path" is unity.

In this context, what is the path? The path leading to hell; the path leading to the animal realm; the path leading to the sphere of hungry ghosts; the path leading to the realm of asuras; the path leading to heaven; the path leading to the human world; the path leading to Nibbāna. This is the diversity.
“Cessation” means oneness.
In this context, what is cessation?

It is cessation through deliberation, cessation not through deliberation, cessation of attachment, cessation of aversion, cessation of conceit, cessation of hypocrisy, cessation of spite, cessation of envy, cessation of avarice, and the cessation of all defilements.
This is diversity.
"Form" is unity.
In this regard, what is form?
Material form consisting of the four great elements is the designation for form derived from the four great elements.
In this context, what are the four great elements?
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
One comprehends the elements in two ways: by way of summary and by way of detail. How does one comprehend the elements in detail?
One comprehends the earth element in detail by way of twenty aspects, and the water element by way of twelve aspects.
He comprehends in detail; he comprehends the fire element in detail by way of four aspects;
he comprehends the air element in detail by way of six aspects.
By which twenty aspects does he comprehend the earth element in detail?
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver,
midriff, spleen, lungs, bowels, entrails, gorge, dung, and brain in the head"—
in these twenty aspects he comprehends the earth element in detail.
In what twelve aspects does one comprehend the water element in detail?
There is bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, and urine in this body; it is in these twelve aspects that one comprehends the water element in detail.
In what four aspects does one comprehend the fire element in detail?

One comprehends the fire element in detail by way of these four aspects: that by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper digestion.
By way of which six aspects does one comprehend the air element in detail?

Upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds in the stomach, winds in the intestines, winds that course through the various limbs, and inhalation and exhalation—by way of these six aspects, one comprehends the air element in detail.
Thus, by means of these forty-two modes, examining, weighing, scrutinizing, fathoming, and reviewing the elements according to their intrinsic nature,
one does not perceive anything fit to be grasped— neither a body nor a portion of a body— just as, for example,
one who sifts through a cesspool would not perceive anything fit to be grasped. Just as...
Just as one sifting through a refuse heap might see nothing worth taking, just as one sifting through a privy might see nothing worth taking,
or just as one sifting through a charnel ground might see nothing worth taking—
so too, by means of these forty-two aspects, one characterizes the elements according to their intrinsic nature in detail.
Weighing it, examining it, fathoming it, and reviewing it, one does not see anything to be grasped, whether it be the body or any part of the body.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply the earth element."
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—thus should it be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and detaches the mind from the earth element.
And as for the internal water element and the external water element... [and so on].
Now, both the internal fire element and the external fire element—and likewise both the internal air element and the external air element—are simply the air element.
One should regard this with right wisdom, as it actually is: "This is not mine; this I am not; this is not my self."
It is to be seen; having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and detaches the mind from the air element.
This is its diversity.
"Ignorance" is its unity.

In this context, what is ignorance? It is lack of knowledge regarding suffering, lack of knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, lack of knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, lack of knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,
lack of knowledge regarding the past, lack of knowledge regarding the future, and lack of knowledge regarding both the past and the future.
Ignorance regarding phenomena that are dependently originated through specific conditionality—

whatever such ignorance is, non-seeing, non-comprehension, non-awakening, non-enlightenment, non-penetration, lack of observation, lack of close observation, lack of repeated observation, lack of reflection,
lack of direct confrontation, dullness, folly, lack of clear comprehension, delusion, extreme delusion, and total delusion.

Ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the underlying tendency to ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the snare of ignorance, delusion, and the unwholesome root— this is diversity.
"True knowledge" is unity.
In this context, what is true knowledge (*vijjā*)?
It is knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering;
knowledge of the past, knowledge of the future, knowledge of both the past and the future; and knowledge of specific conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.
Knowledge regarding phenomena; that which is such wisdom, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation, investigation of phenomena,
discernment, close examination, comparative examination, sagacity, skill, subtlety, discrimination, reflection, scrutiny, breadth,
intelligence, guidance, insight, clear comprehension, the goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom.
Wisdom as a sword, wisdom as a palace, wisdom as light, wisdom as radiance, wisdom as a lamp, wisdom as a jewel, non-delusion,
investigation of phenomena, right view, the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is the diversity.
“Attainment” (*samāpatti*) means oneness.
In this context, what is attainment?
It is the attainment of perception, the attainment of non-perception, and the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The attainment of the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the attainment of cessation—
this is their diversity.
"One who meditates"— this is their unity.
In this regard, who is a meditator?

There is the meditator who is a trainee (sekha), there is the meditator who is one beyond training (asekha), there is the meditator who is neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training, the noble-bred meditator, the wild-horse meditator, the meditator who has overcome views, the meditator who has overcome craving, and the meditator who has overcome wisdom.
This is the diversity.
“Concentration” means one-pointedness.
In this context, what is concentration?
Concentration with conflict, concentration without conflict; concentration with enmity, concentration without enmity; concentration with ill will, concentration without ill will.
Concentration free from affliction; concentration accompanied by rapture; concentration free from rapture; concentration with the material;
concentration without the material; concentration with volitional effort; concentration without volitional effort;

concentration developed in one way; concentration developed in both ways; concentration whose development has been completed in both ways; concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought alone.
Concentration, concentration without applied thought and sustained thought, concentration partaking of diminution, concentration partaking of stagnation, concentration partaking of distinction,
concentration partaking of penetration, worldly concentration, supramundane concentration, wrong concentration, and right concentration. This is the diversity.
“Practice” (*paṭipadā*) means oneness.
In this regard, what is practice?
There is the extreme practice, the emaciated practice, the middle practice, the impatient practice, and the patient practice.
The even way of practice, the taming way of practice, the painful way of practice with sluggish direct knowledge, the painful way of practice with swift direct knowledge,
the pleasant way of practice with sluggish direct knowledge, and the pleasant way of practice with swift direct knowledge—
this is the diversity.
“Body” (kāya) means unity.
In this context, what is the body?
It is the mental body (nāmakāya) and the material body (rūpakāya).
In this regard, what is the material body (rūpakāya)?
Head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver,
midriff, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, gorge, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, [blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, and urine].
Blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, urine, and brain matter—
this is the body of form (rūpakāya).
The so-called "body of name" (nāmakāya) consists of feeling, perception, volition, consciousness, contact, and attention.
"This is the body of names"—
this is the diversity.
Thus, whatever phenomenon shares the same nature as another phenomenon, that phenomenon becomes one with that phenomenon through their unity.
But by whatever characteristic it is dissimilar, by that it goes toward diversity.
Thus, when questioned regarding a discourse (sutta), an exposition (veyyākaraṇa), a verse (gāthā), or a question, one should investigate: "Does he ask about unity, or rather about diversity?
If he has asked about unity, it should be answered in terms of unity.
If asked in terms of diversity, it should be answered in terms of diversity.
If asked with reference to beings, it should be answered with reference to beings.
If asked with reference to phenomena, it should be answered with reference to phenomena.
Or rather, one should answer in whatever way one is questioned.
Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "The states are due to their unity.
The Mode of Conveying the Foundation is concluded.
